titre: The Overton Window: A Concept Its Author Never Published
accroche: Cited as a weapon of political manipulation, the Overton window was not published by Overton: all that remains is a sheet from a notepad.
contenu_vulgarise:
On social media, the “Overton window” comes back with every controversy: it is presented as a theory according to which it would be enough to defend extreme positions, even absurd ones, to “shift” what seems acceptable and make more moderate positions look reasonable. The name attached to it, that of Joseph Overton, an executive at an American think tank, gives this theory an academic veneer. The problem: according to *The New Republic*, Overton never put his most influential idea down on paper to circulate it, and he did not even name it.

## A Diagram, Not a Published Theory

In the 1990s, Joseph Overton was senior vice president of the Mackinac Center for Public Policy, a Michigan think tank, where he had worked since 1992. He described a spectrum running from “more freedom” to “less freedom” with respect to state intervention, shown on a vertical axis to avoid comparison with the left-right divide. On this spectrum, he located at a given moment the “window” of policies that a politician can defend without putting himself at risk. For him, it was up to think tanks to propose policies lying outside the window, in order to move it. What survives, according to *Michigan Capitol Confidential*, is a scribbled yellow notepad sheet, on which he spoke simply of a “window of political possibilities”: a working document, not a publication. Overton died on June 30, 2003, at 43, in an ultralight plane accident near Caro, Michigan.

## The Posthumous Name of an Unpublished Idea

It was his colleague Joseph Lehman who, after his death, took up the diagram, developed it, and named it the “Overton window” in his honor. He then taught it to other think tanks. Lehman makes a point that has disappeared from most current uses of the term: according to him, politicians do not move the window, they detect where it is, then line up with it. The term circulates today as if it described a conscious, instantaneous technique of manipulation, whereas the window rather describes the slow evolution of a society's values and norms.

One practical consequence: there is no text by Overton that presents his window under this name. What can be cited is what his colleagues wrote and said about it, Lehman first, after his death.

carte.punch: The “Overton window,” cited as a political weapon, was not published by its author.
carte.idee: In the 1990s, Joseph Overton devised a diagram to locate acceptable policies at a given moment; he did not name it and left no publication on it. He died in 2003; it is his colleague Lehman who named and spread the concept after the fact.
carte.source_courte: Wikipedia; The New Republic; Mich. Capitol Confidential

quiz.question: Why is there no text by Overton presenting his “window” under that name?
choix: Because Overton did not name his idea; a colleague named and spread it after his death
Because the Mackinac Center's archives were destroyed in a fire after 2003
Because Overton wrote under a pseudonym that no one has been able to identify with certainty
Because the concept was first published in secret and then withdrawn from circulation by the think tank
quiz.explication: Overton devised a diagram without naming it; it was his colleague Joseph Lehman who named it and explained it publicly after his death in 2003, not a fire, a pseudonym, or a retraction.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what axis does Overton present his spectrum, and why?
choix: On a horizontal axis, to make it easier to read on a notepad sheet
On a circular axis, to represent the spectrum's internal contradictions
On a vertical axis, to avoid comparison with the left-right divide
On a chronological axis, to show the evolution of his own opinions
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the vertical axis was chosen by Overton to avoid equating his spectrum with the usual left-right divide.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does a politician do in the face of the Overton window, according to Joseph Lehman?
choix: He deliberately moves it by defending extreme positions
He detects where it is, then lines up with it, without moving it himself
He publishes it officially to inform citizens of its limits
He ignores it and follows only the opinion polls of the moment
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Lehman specifies that politicians do not move the window: they spot where it is and conform to it, contrary to the common use of the term.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What position did Joseph Overton hold at the Mackinac Center before his death?
choix: Founder and president of the think tank since its creation
Director of communications, in charge of press relations
Visiting professor of political science seconded by a university
Senior vice president, where he had worked since 1992
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that Overton was senior vice president of the Mackinac Center for Public Policy, where he had worked since 1992, until his death in 2003.
